content:
Lists of contradictions in the Quran circulate widely online, often with dozens of entries. Most rest on a small number of patterns: numbers that seem not to add up, time spans that seem to clash, and acts attributed to more than one agent.

The lists grow long because the same few patterns repeat. A verse is read in a translation that flattens a distinction the Arabic keeps. Two verses about different events are treated as statements about one. A general statement and a particular one are set side by side as if the second denied the first. Muslim scholars met every one of these patterns early, and wrote whole books about them. Ibn Qutayba of Baghdad, who died in 889, devoted his Ta'wil Mushkil al-Quran to verses that seem difficult or that appear to clash, and in the twentieth century the Mauritanian scholar Muhammad al-Amin al-Shinqiti wrote a book whose title announces its subject: the removal of the illusion of contradiction from the verses of the Book.[1]

The four points below take the Quran's own test and three of the best-known cases, with the answers the classical commentators gave.

The Quran asks whether people do not reflect on it, and states that had it come from anyone other than God, they would have found much inconsistency in it.[2] Critics take up the challenge and present lists of verses that appear to clash. The classical commentators met the same questions centuries earlier, and recorded their answers.

The questions are older than the commentaries. Al-Bukhari records that a man came to Ibn Abbas, the cousin of the Prophet, and said, "I find things in the Quran that seem to differ to me." He listed them. One verse says that on the Day of Resurrection people will not ask after one another, and another that they will turn to one another asking. One verse says that the guilty will hide nothing from God, and another that they will swear they were never polytheists. One passage puts the creation of the earth before the heaven, and another the heaven before the earth.[3]

Ibn Abbas answered each in turn. The Day has stages, so the people are silent at one stage and question each other at another. The polytheists deny at first, and then their mouths are sealed and their limbs speak, so in the end nothing is hidden. The answer on creation is given under the next entry. He closed with a rule for reading: let nothing in the Quran seem to you to differ, for all of it is from God.[3] The report shows that the first generation read the Quran closely enough to notice these tensions, and that it resolved them from the text.

The word the Quran uses in 4:82 matters too. Ikhtilaf kathir means much divergence: a text that contradicts itself in its reports, its rulings and its quality. The commentators read the verse as a claim about the whole book, revealed over twenty-three years in changing circumstances, which nonetheless holds together in what it says about God, the prophets and the moral law.[4] A critic who finds one hard verse has found a question. The verse invites the reader to try the larger test, and the critics who take it up rarely do.

One pattern deserves a word on its own. Some lists count abrogation as contradiction: a ruling given at one time and replaced at another. The Quran states openly that God replaces one verse with another, and the jurists treated the change as a matter of timing and law.[5] Two rulings in force at different times are a sequence, and the Quran names it as one. The article on abrogation and the Sword Verse takes that subject further.

Three of the most frequently cited cases are set out below, each with the reconciliation the commentators gave.

One passage says that God created the earth in two days, set mountains on it, blessed it and measured out its provisions in four days, and then formed the seven heavens in two days.[6] Added together, that seems to make eight days, while other verses speak of the heavens and earth created in six.[7]

Al-Tabari recorded the explanation of a grammarian of Basra: the four days include the first two, as a man might say that he married one woman yesterday and two today, one of whom was yesterday's bride. On this reading the earth and its provisions take four days in total and the heavens two, which makes six.[8] The commentators read the verse this way from the start, so the reconciliation predates the modern objection.

A related question sets 41:9 to 12, where the earth is created before the heavens, against 79:27 to 30, which describes the building of the heaven and then says, "and the earth, after that, He spread it out." This was the third question put to Ibn Abbas, and his answer is recorded with it. God created the earth in two days, then turned to the heaven and formed it in two days, then spread out the earth in two days, bringing out its water and pasture and setting the mountains. The verb in 79:30, daha, means to spread out, so the creation of the earth came first and its spreading came after the heaven. That gives the earth four days in all and the heavens two.[3]

The strongest form of the objection calls this special pleading: a reader who meets eight days has to invent a way of making six. The answer is that both explanations come from the earliest layer of interpretation, and that the arithmetic of Ibn Abbas and the grammarian of Basra arrives at the same total by different routes. Arabic counts inclusively in just this way when a sum is given for a whole task, and the phrase "in four days, alike for those who ask" gives a total for the earth and its provisions together. The word day itself, yawm, is used in the Quran for a span whose length God sets, as the next entry shows.[9]

One verse says that a day with God is like a thousand years of human reckoning, another that God's command ascends to him in a day whose measure is a thousand years, and a third that the angels and the Spirit ascend to him in a day whose measure is fifty thousand years.[9]

The verses describe different things. Ibn Kathir recorded four views of the fifty-thousand-year day, among them the report from Ibn Abbas that it measures the full span of God's command from the lowest earth to above the heavens, while the thousand-year day measures its descent from the sky to the earth and its return.[10] Al-Qurtubi added the view of several early authorities that the fifty-thousand-year day is the Day of Resurrection, which for the unbelievers will seem to last that long.[11] A day of one length and a day of another, said of different events, contradict nothing.

The strongest form of the objection notes that 32:5 and 70:4 both use the verb to ascend, and argues that they must describe one journey. The subjects differ. In 32:5 it is the command of God that descends and ascends. In 70:4 it is the angels and the Spirit. The verse in 70:4 also belongs to a passage about the punishment of the unbelievers, which is why so many early authorities read its day as the Day of Resurrection.[11] Different subjects, different journeys and different contexts give different measures.

The Bible uses the same image. The Second Letter of Peter tells its readers not to forget that "with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day", echoing Psalm 90.[12] No Christian reader takes that to fix the length of every day God speaks of. The Quran uses the same figure in 22:47, in answer to those who asked for the punishment to be hurried, and it uses the figure of fifty thousand in a different passage for a different purpose.

The Quran says that God takes the souls at the time of their death,[13] that the angel of death who is put in charge of people takes them,[14] and that God's messengers take a person when death comes.[15] Critics ask which is true.

All three are, in the way that a ruler and his officers can each be said to act. Al-Tabari read the first verse as a proof of God's sole power to give life and death,[16] and the other verses name the angels who carry out that decree: one angel in charge of death and the messengers who act with him. The Quran attributes the act to God as its source and to the angels as its agents.

The Quran uses this double attribution openly elsewhere, and in a form that rules out the charge of confusion. Of the battle of Badr it says to the Prophet, "you did not throw when you threw, but it was God who threw".[17] The throwing is affirmed of the Prophet and of God in a single sentence. A writer who did not know he was doing it could not write that sentence. The verses on death follow the same pattern: God decrees and takes, the angel of death is charged with it, and the angels who serve him carry it out. Other verses describe those angels at work, striking the faces and backs of the unbelievers as they take them.[18]

The strongest form of the objection is that a single author would have chosen one way of speaking. A single author with a doctrine of secondary causes would do exactly what the Quran does. Human languages speak this way constantly: a king builds a city that his workers built, and a judge sentences a man whom an officer then takes away. The Quran adds a theological reason. Everything that happens comes from God, so every act may be named as His, and the agents He uses may be named as theirs.

The bottom line

The cases in the long lists fall into a few patterns, and the commentators answered each pattern from the text. The days of creation add up once the Arabic is read as Arabic. The days of a thousand and fifty thousand years measure different things. The taking of souls is ascribed to God and to His angels in the way the Quran ascribes the throwing at Badr to God and to the Prophet. None of the answers is modern, and several go back to Ibn Abbas.

A reader may still find a verse hard, and the Muslim tradition has never pretended otherwise. It has kept the questions alongside the answers, from the man who came to Ibn Abbas to the books of Ibn Qutayba and al-Shinqiti. The challenge of 4:82 asks for much divergence, in a book revealed over twenty-three years. The best-known cases on the lists do not supply it.
